{{Short description|Subset of a graph's nodes such that all other nodes link to at least one}}
{{For|Dominator in control flow graphs|Dominator (graph theory)}}

[[File:Dominating-set.svg|frame|right|Three dominating sets of the same graph (in red). The domination number of this graph is 2: (b) and (c) show that there is a dominating set with 2 vertices, and there is no dominating set with only 1 vertex.]]

In [[graph theory]], a '''dominating set''' for a [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] {{math|1=''G''}} is a subset {{math|1=''D''}} of its vertices, such that any vertex of {{math|1=''G''}} is in {{math|1=''D''}}, or has a neighbor in {{math|1=''D''}}. The '''domination number''' {{math|γ(''G'')}} is the number of vertices in a smallest dominating set for {{mvar|G}}.

The '''dominating set problem''' concerns testing whether {{math|γ(''G'') ≤ ''K''}} for a given graph {{mvar|G}} and input {{mvar|K}}; it is a classical [[NP-complete]] [[decision problem]] in [[computational complexity theory]].{{sfnp|Garey|Johnson|1979}} Therefore it is believed that there may be no [[polynomial-time algorithm|efficient algorithm]] that can compute {{math|γ(''G'')}} for all graphs {{math|1=''G''}}. However, there are efficient [[approximation algorithm]]s, as well as efficient exact algorithms for certain graph classes.

Dominating sets are of practical interest in several areas. In [[wireless networking]], dominating sets are used to find efficient routes within ad-hoc mobile networks. They have also been used in [[document summarization]], and in designing secure systems for [[Electrical grid|electrical grids]].

Dominating sets are closely related to [[Independent set (graph theory)|independent set]]s: an independent set is also a dominating set [[if and only if]] it is a [[maximal independent set]], so any maximal independent set in a graph is necessarily also a minimal dominating set.

== Formal definition ==
Given an undirected graph {{math|1=''G'' = (''V'', ''E'')}}, a [[subset]] of vertices <math>D\subseteq V</math> is called a '''dominating set''' if for every vertex <math>u\in V\setminus D</math>, there is a vertex <math>v\in D</math> such that <math>\{u,v\} \in E</math>.  

Every graph has at least one dominating set: if <math>D=V=</math> the set of all vertices, then by definition ''D'' is a dominating set, since there is no vertex <math>u\in V\setminus D</math>. A more interesting challenge is to find small dominating sets. The '''domination number''' of {{math|1=''G''}} is defined as:  <math>\gamma(G) := \min \{|D| : D \text{ is a dominating set of } G \}</math>.

==History==

The domination problem was studied from the 1950s onwards, but the rate of research on domination significantly increased in the mid-1970s. In 1972, [[Richard Karp]] proved the [[set cover problem]] to be [[NP-complete]]. This had immediate implications for the dominating set problem, as there are straightforward vertex to set and edge to non-disjoint-intersection bijections between the two problems. This proved the dominating set problem to be [[NP-complete]] as well.{{sfnp|Hedetniemi|Laskar|1990}}

== Algorithms and computational complexity ==

The set cover problem is a well-known [[NP-hard]] problem – the decision version of set covering was one of [[Karp's 21 NP-complete problems]]. There exist a pair of polynomial-time [[L-reduction]]s between the minimum dominating set problem and the [[set cover problem]].{{sfnp|Kann|1992|pp=108–109}} These reductions ([[#L-reductions|see below]]) show that an efficient algorithm for the minimum dominating set problem would provide an efficient algorithm for the set cover problem, and vice versa. Moreover, the reductions preserve the [[approximation algorithm|approximation ratio]]: for any α, a polynomial-time {{nowrap|α-approximation}} algorithm for minimum dominating sets would provide a polynomial-time {{nowrap|α-approximation}} algorithm for the set cover problem and vice versa. Both problems are in fact [[APX#Related complexity classes|Log-APX-complete]].{{sfnp|Escoffier|Paschos|2006}}

The approximability of set covering is also well understood: a logarithmic approximation factor can be found by using a [[Set cover problem#Greedy algorithm|simple greedy algorithm]], and finding a sublogarithmic approximation factor is NP-hard. More specifically, the greedy algorithm provides a factor {{math|1 + log{{abs|''V''}}}} approximation of a minimum dominating set, and no polynomial time algorithm can achieve an approximation factor better than {{math|''c'' log{{abs|''V''}}}} for some {{math|''c'' > 0}} unless [[P = NP]].{{sfnp|Raz|Safra|1997}}

===L-reductions===

The following two reductions show that the minimum dominating set problem and the [[set cover problem]] are equivalent under [[L-reduction]]s: given an instance of one problem, we can construct an equivalent instance of the other problem.{{sfnp|Kann|1992|pp=108–109}}

====From dominating set to set covering====
Given a graph {{math|1=''G'' = (''V'', ''E'')}} with {{math|1=''V'' = {1, 2, ..., ''n''},}} construct a set cover instance {{math|(''U'', ''S'')}} as follows: the [[Universe (mathematics)|universe]] {{mvar|U}} is {{mvar|V}}, and the family of subsets is {{math|1=''S'' = {''S''{{sub|1}}, ''S''{{sub|2}}, ..., ''S''{{sub|''n''}}} }} such that {{mvar|S{{sub|v}}}} consists of the vertex {{mvar|v}} and all vertices adjacent to {{mvar|v}} in {{mvar|G}}.

Now if {{mvar|D}} is a dominating set for {{mvar|G}}, then {{math|1=''C'' = {''S''{{sub|''v''}} : ''v'' ∈ ''D''} }} is a feasible solution of the set cover problem, with {{math|1={{abs|''C''}} = {{abs|''D''}}}}. Conversely, if {{math|1=''C'' = {''S''{{sub|''v''}} : ''v'' ∈ ''D''} }} is a feasible solution of the set cover problem, then {{mvar|D}} is a dominating set for {{mvar|G}}, with {{math|1={{abs|''D''}} = {{abs|''C''}}}}.

Hence the size of a minimum dominating set for {{mvar|G}} equals the size of a minimum set cover for {{math|(''U'', ''S'')}}. Furthermore, there is a simple algorithm that maps a dominating set to a set cover of the same size and vice versa. In particular, an efficient {{nowrap|α-approximation}} algorithm for set covering provides an efficient {{nowrap|α-approximation}} algorithm for minimum dominating sets.

[[File:Dominating-set-2.svg|right]]
::For example, given the graph {{mvar|G}} shown on the right, we construct a set cover instance with the universe {{math|1=''U'' = {1, 2, ..., 6} }} and the subsets {{math|1=''S''{{sub|1}} = {1, 2, 5},}} {{math|1=''S''{{sub|2}} = {1, 2, 3, 5},}} {{math|1=''S''{{sub|3}} = {2, 3, 4, 6},}} {{math|1=''S''{{sub|4}} = {3, 4},}} {{math|1=''S''{{sub|5}} = {1, 2, 5, 6},}} and {{math|1=''S''{{sub|6}} = {3, 5, 6}.}} In this example, {{math|1=''D'' = {3, 5} }} is a dominating set for {{mvar|G}} – this corresponds to the set cover {{math|1=''C'' = {''S''{{sub|3}}, ''S''{{sub|5}}}.}} For example, the vertex {{math|4 ∈ ''V''}} is dominated by the vertex {{math|3 ∈ ''D''}}, and the element {{math|4 ∈ ''U''}} is contained in the set {{math|''S''{{sub|3}} ∈ ''C''}}.

====From set covering to dominating set====
Let {{math|1=(''S'', ''U'')}} be an instance of the set cover problem with the universe {{mvar|U}} and the family of subsets {{math|1=''S'' = {''S''{{sub|''i''}} : ''i'' ∈ ''I''};}} we assume that {{mvar|U}} and the index set {{mvar|I}} are disjoint. Construct a graph {{math|1=''G'' = (''V'', ''E'')}} as follows: the set of vertices is {{math|1=''V'' = ''I'' ∪ ''U''}}, there is an edge {{math|{''i'', ''j''} ∈ ''E''}} between each pair {{math|1=''i'', ''j'' ∈ ''I''}}, and there is also an edge {{math|{''i'', ''u''} }} for each {{math|''i'' ∈ ''I''}} and {{math|''u'' ∈ ''S''{{sub|''i''}}}}. That is, {{mvar|G}} is a [[split graph]]: {{mvar|I}} is a [[Clique (graph theory)|clique]] and {{mvar|U}} is an [[Independent set (graph theory)|independent set]].

Now if {{math|1=''C'' = {''S''{{sub|''i''}} : ''i'' ∈ ''D''} }} is a feasible solution of the set cover problem for some subset {{math|''D'' ⊆ ''I''}}, then {{mvar|D}} is a dominating set for {{mvar|G}}, with {{math|1={{abs|''D''}} = {{abs|''C''}}}}: First, for each {{math|''u'' ∈ ''U''}} there is an {{math|''i'' ∈ ''D''}} such that {{math|''u'' ∈ ''S''{{sub|''i''}}}}, and by construction, {{mvar|u}} and {{mvar|i}} are adjacent in {{mvar|G}}; hence {{mvar|u}} is dominated by {{mvar|i}}. Second, since {{mvar|D}} must be nonempty, each {{math|''i'' ∈ ''I''}} is adjacent to a vertex in {{mvar|D}}.

Conversely, let {{mvar|D}} be a dominating set for {{mvar|G}}. Then it is possible to construct another dominating set {{mvar|X}} such that {{math|{{abs|''X''}} ≤ {{abs|''D''}}}} and {{math|''X'' ⊆ ''I''}}: simply replace each {{math|''u'' ∈ ''D'' ∩ ''U''}} by a neighbour {{math|''i'' ∈ ''I''}} of {{mvar|u}}. Then {{math|1=''C'' = {''S''{{sub|''i''}} : ''i'' ∈ ''X''} }} is a feasible solution of the set cover problem, with {{math|1={{abs|''C''}} = {{abs|''X''}} ≤ {{abs|''D''}}}}.

[[File:Dominating-set-reduction.svg|right]]
::The illustration on the right show the construction for {{math|1=''U'' = {''a'', ''b'', ''c'', ''d'', ''e''}, ''I'' = {1, 2, 3, 4},}} {{math|1=''S''{{sub|1}} = {''a'', ''b'', ''c''},}} {{math|1=''S''{{sub|2}} = {''a'', ''b''},}} {{math|1=''S''{{sub|3}} = {''b'', ''c'', ''d''},}} and {{math|1=''S''{{sub|4}} = {''c'', ''d'', ''e''}.}}

::In this example, {{math|1=''C'' = {''S''{{sub|1}}, ''S''{{sub|4}}} }} is a set cover; this corresponds to the dominating set {{math|1=''D'' = {1, 4}.}}

::{{math|1=''D'' = {''a'', 3, 4} }} is another dominating set for the graph {{mvar|G}}. Given {{mvar|D}}, we can construct a dominating set {{math|1=''X'' = {1, 3, 4} }} which is not larger than {{mvar|D}} and which is a subset of {{mvar|I}}. The dominating set {{mvar|X}} corresponds to the set cover {{math|1=''C'' = {''S''{{sub|1}}, ''S''{{sub|3}}, ''S''{{sub|4}}}.}}

===Special cases===

If the graph has maximum degree Δ, then the greedy approximation algorithm finds an {{math|''O''(log Δ)}}-approximation of a minimum dominating set. Also, let {{mvar|d{{sub|g}}}} be the [[cardinality]] of dominating set obtained using greedy approximation then following relation holds, <math> d_g \le N+1 - \sqrt{2M+1}</math>, where {{mvar|N}} is number of nodes and {{mvar|M}} is number of edges in given undirected graph.{{sfnp|Parekh|1991}} For fixed Δ, this qualifies as a dominating set for [[APX]] membership; in fact, it is APX-complete.{{sfnp|Papadimitriou|Yannakakis|1991}}

The problem admits a [[polynomial-time approximation scheme]] (PTAS) for special cases such as [[unit disk graph]]s and [[planar graph]]s.{{sfnp|Crescenzi|Kann|Halldórsson|Karpinski|2000}} A minimum dominating set can be found in linear time in [[series–parallel graph]]s.{{sfnp|Takamizawa|Nishizeki|Saito|1982}}

===Exact algorithms===

A minimum dominating set of an {{mvar|n}}-vertex graph can be found in time {{math|''O''(2{{sup|''n''}}''n'')}} by inspecting all vertex subsets. {{harvtxt|Fomin|Grandoni|Kratsch|2009}} show how to find a minimum dominating set in time {{math|''O''(1.5137{{sup|''n''}})}} and exponential space, and in time {{math|''O''(1.5264{{sup|''n''}})}} and polynomial space. A faster algorithm, using {{math|''O''(1.5048{{sup|''n''}})}} time was found by {{harvtxt|van Rooij|Nederlof|van Dijk|2009}}, who also show that the number of minimum dominating sets can be computed in this time.  The number of minimal dominating sets is at most {{math|1.7159{{sup|''n''}}}} and all such sets can be listed in time  {{math|''O''(1.7159{{sup|''n''}})}}.{{sfnp|Fomin|Grandoni|Pyatkin|Stepanov|2008}}

===Parameterized complexity===

Finding a dominating set of size {{mvar|k}} plays a central role in the theory of parameterized complexity. It is the most well-known problem complete for the class [[W(2)|W[2] ]] and used in many reductions to show intractability of other problems. In particular, the problem is not [[fixed-parameter tractable]] in the sense that no algorithm with running time {{math|''f''(''k'')''n''{{sup|O(1)}}}} for any function {{mvar|f}} exists unless the W-hierarchy collapses to FPT=W[2].

On the other hand, if the input graph is planar, the problem remains NP-hard, but a fixed-parameter algorithm is known. In fact, the problem has a kernel of size linear in {{mvar|k}},{{sfnp|Alber|Fellows|Niedermeier|2004}} and running times that are exponential in {{radic|''k''}} and cubic in {{mvar|n}} may be obtained by applying [[dynamic programming]] to a [[branch-decomposition]] of the kernel.{{sfnp|Fomin|Thilikos|2006}} More generally, the dominating set problem and many variants of the problem are fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by both the size of the dominating set and the size of the smallest [[forbidden graph characterization|forbidden]] [[complete bipartite graph|complete bipartite subgraph]]; that is, the problem is FPT on [[biclique-free graph]]s, a very general class of sparse graphs that includes the planar graphs.{{sfnp|Telle|Villanger|2012}}

The complementary set to a dominating set, a [[nonblocker]], can be found by a fixed-parameter algorithm on any graph.{{sfnp|Dehne|Fellows|Fernau|Prieto|2006}}

== Variants ==

An '''[[independent dominating set]]''' is a dominating set that is also an [[Independent set (graph theory)|independent set]], or equivalently, a [[maximal independent set]]. The '''independent domination number''' <math>i(G)</math> is the minimum size of an independent dominating set of {{mvar|G}}. Since the minimum is taken over fewer sets, <math>\gamma(G) \leq i(G)</math> for all graphs {{mvar|G}}, and the inequality can be strict. Equality holds for [[claw-free graph]]s;{{sfnp|Allan|Laskar|1978}} since every [[line graph]] is claw-free, it follows that the minimum [[maximal matching]] and the minimum [[edge dominating set]] of any graph have the same size.

An '''[[independence dominating set]]''' of a graph <math>G</math> is a set that dominates every [[Independent set (graph theory)|independent set]] of <math>G</math>. The '''independence domination number''' <math>i\gamma(G)</math> is the maximum, over all independent sets <math>A</math> of <math>G</math>, of the smallest set dominating <math>A</math>.{{sfnp|Aharoni|Berger|Ziv|2007}} Dominating only independent sets requires potentially fewer vertices than dominating all vertices, so <math>i\gamma(G) \leq \gamma(G)</math> for all graphs <math>G</math>, and the ratio <math>\gamma(G) / i\gamma(G)</math> can be arbitrarily large.{{sfnp|Aharoni|Berger|Ziv|2007}}

A '''[[connected dominating set]]''' is a dominating set that is also [[Connected (graph theory)|connected]]. If <math>S</math> is a connected dominating set, one can form a [[spanning tree]] of <math>G</math> in which <math>S</math> forms the set of non-leaf vertices of the tree; conversely, if <math>T</math> is any spanning tree in a graph with more than two vertices, the non-leaf vertices of <math>T</math> form a connected dominating set. Therefore, finding minimum connected dominating sets is equivalent to finding spanning trees with the maximum possible number of leaves.

A '''total dominating set''' is a set of vertices such that all vertices in the graph, ''including'' the vertices in the dominating set themselves, have a neighbor in the dominating set.{{sfnp|West|2001|loc = Section 3.1}} That is: for every vertex <math>u\in V</math>, there is a vertex <math>v\in D</math> such that <math>\{u,v\} \in E</math>. Figure (c) above shows a dominating set that is a connected dominating set and a total dominating set; the examples in figures (a) and (b) are neither. In contrast to a simple dominating set, a total dominating set may not exist. For example, a graph with one or more vertices and no edges does not have a total dominating set. The '''total domination number''' <math>\gamma^\text{total}(G)</math> is defined as the minimum size of a total dominating set of {{math|1=''G''}}; obviously, <math>\gamma^\text{total}(G) \geq \gamma(G)</math>.

A '''dominating edge-set''' is a set of edges (vertex pairs) whose union is a dominating set; such a set may not exist (for example, a graph with one or more vertices and no edges does not have it). If it exists, then the union of all its edges is a total dominating set. Therefore, the smallest size of an edge-dominating set is at least <math>\gamma^\text{total}(G) /2</math>.

In contrast, an [[Edge dominating set|'''edge-dominating set''']] is a set <math>D</math> of edges, such that every edge not in <math>D</math> is adjacent to at least one edge in <math>D</math>; such a set always exists (for example, the set of all edges is an edge-dominating set).

A '''{{mvar|k}}-dominating set''' is a set of vertices such that each vertex not in the set has at least {{mvar|k}} neighbors in the set (a standard dominating set is a 1-dominating set). Similarly, a '''{{mvar|k}}-tuple dominating set''' is a set of vertices such that each vertex in the graph has at least {{mvar|k}} neighbors in the set (a total dominating set is a 1-tuple dominating set). An {{math|(1&thinsp;+&nbsp;log ''n'')}}-approximation of a minimum {{mvar|k}}-[[tuple]] dominating set can be found in polynomial time.{{sfnp|Klasing|Laforest|2004}} Every graph admits a {{mvar|k}}-dominating set (for example, the set of all vertices); but only graphs with minimum degree {{math|''k'' − 1}} admit a {{mvar|k}}-tuple dominating set. However, even if the graph admits {{mvar|k}}-tuple dominating set, a minimum {{mvar|k}}-tuple dominating set can be nearly {{mvar|k}} times as large as a minimum {{mvar|k}}-dominating set for the same graph;{{sfnp|Förster|2013}} An {{math|(1.7 + log Δ)}}-approximation of a minimum {{mvar|k}}-dominating set can be found in polynomial time as well.

A '''[[fractional dominating set]]''' is defined from a ''fractional dominating function'', a function <math>f: V(G) \to [0, 1]</math> such that for every vertex <math>v \in V</math>, the sum of <math>f</math> over the [[neighborhood (graph theory)|closed neighborhood]] <math>N[v]</math> is at least 1.{{sfnp|Haynes|Hedetniemi|Slater|1998}} The '''fractional domination number''' <math>\gamma_f(G)</math> is the minimum total weight (sum of all vertex values) of such a function, and satisfies <math>\gamma_f(G) \leq \gamma(G)</math>. For a <math>k</math>-[[regular graph]] with <math>n</math> vertices (<math>k \geq 1</math>), the fractional domination number equals <math>n/(k+1)</math>.

A '''star-dominating set'''  is a [[subset]] <math>D</math> of <math>V</math> such that, for every vertex <math>v</math> in <math>V</math>, the [[Star (graph theory)|star]] of <math>v</math> (the set of edges adjacent to <math>v</math>) intersects the star of some vertex in <math>D</math>. Clearly, if <math>G</math> has [[Isolated vertex|isolated vertices]] then it has no star-dominating sets (since the star of isolated vertices is empty). If <math>G</math> has no isolated vertices, then every dominating set is a star-dominating set and vice versa. The distinction between star-domination and usual domination is more substantial when their fractional variants are considered.{{sfnp|Meshulam|2003}}

A '''[[domatic partition]]''' is a partition of the vertices into disjoint dominating sets. The domatic number is the maximum size of a domatic partition.

An '''[[eternal dominating set]]''' is a dynamic version of domination in which a vertex <math>v</math> in dominating set <math>D</math> is chosen and replaced with a neighbor <math>u</math> (<math>u</math> is not in <math>D</math>) such that the modified <math>D</math> is also a dominating set and this process can be repeated over any infinite sequence of choices of vertices&nbsp;<math>v</math>.

An '''[[efficient dominating set]]''' (also called an e.d. set or independent perfect dominating set{{sfnp|Bange|Barkauskas|Slater|1988}}) is a dominating set with the additional property that every vertex in the graph is dominated by '''exactly one''' vertex in the set.{{sfnp|Brandstädt|Leitert|Rautenbach|2012}}

A '''[[Roman dominating set]]''' is defined through a ''Roman dominating function'', which assigns to each vertex a value from <math>\{0, 1, 2\}</math> such that every vertex assigned 0 is adjacent to at least one vertex assigned 2. The '''Roman domination number''' <math>\gamma_R(G)</math> is the minimum sum of all vertex values over all such functions. The concept is inspired by a defensive strategy of the Roman Empire, where vertices represent cities and values represent stationed legions. For any graph <math>G</math>, <math>\gamma(G) \leq \gamma_R(G) \leq 2\gamma(G)</math>, with the lower bound achieved only by the [[empty graph]].{{sfnp|Cockayne|Dreyer|Hedetniemi|Hedetniemi|2004}}

A '''[[global dominating set]]''' is a dominating set of a graph <math>G</math> that is also a dominating set of the [[complement graph]] <math>\overline{G}</math>. The '''global domination number''' <math>\gamma_g(G)</math> is the minimum cardinality of a global dominating set. Equivalently, a dominating set <math>S</math> is a global dominating set if and only if for each vertex <math>v \in V - S</math>, there exists a vertex <math>u \in S</math> such that <math>u</math> is not adjacent to <math>v</math>. By definition, <math>\gamma_g(G) = \gamma_g\big(\overline{G}\big)</math> and <math>\gamma(G) \leq \gamma_g(G)</math>. For a graph <math>G</math> with <math>p</math> vertices, <math>\gamma_g(G) = p</math> if and only if <math>G = K_p</math> or <math>G = \overline{K_p}</math>.{{sfnp|Sampathkumar|1989}}

A '''[[certified dominating set]]''' is a dominating set in which every vertex in the set has either zero or at least two neighbours outside the set.{{sfnp|Dettlaff|Lemańska|Topp|Ziemann|2020}} The '''certified domination number''' <math>\gamma_{\text{cer}}(G)</math> is the minimum size of a certified dominating set. Clearly, <math>\gamma_{\text{cer}}(G) \geq \gamma(G)</math>, and equality holds whenever the graph has no ''weak [[support vertex]]'' (in particular, when <math>\delta(G) \geq 2</math>). For a connected graph, <math>\gamma_{\text{cer}}(G) \leq 2\gamma(G)</math>.

A '''[[paired dominating set]]''' of a graph <math>G = (V, E)</math> is a dominating set <math>S</math> of vertices such that the [[induced subgraph]] <math>G[S]</math> contains at least one [[perfect matching]].{{sfnp|Haynes|Slater|1998}} The '''paired domination number''' <math>\gamma_p(G)</math> is the minimum cardinality of a paired dominating set of <math>G</math>. The concept models a situation in which guards are placed at vertices of a graph to dominate (protect) all vertices, with the additional constraint that each guard is assigned another adjacent guard as a backup.

Other variants include
* restrained dominating set,{{sfnp|Domke|Hattingh|Hedetniemi|Laskar|1999}}
* secure dominating set,{{sfnp|Merouane|Chellali|2015}}
* triple connected dominating set,{{sfnp|Mahadevan|Avadayappan|Joseph|Subramanian|2012}}
* signed dominating set,{{sfnp|Haas|Wexler|2004}}
* minus dominating set,{{sfnp|Kang|Shan|2020}} and
* friendly dominating set.{{sfnp|Cabahug Jr.|Eballe|Fernandez|2025}}
